chunks.text: Bael (Aegle marmelos) is the only species in the monotypic genus Aegle, in the citrus family Rutaceae (order Sapindales, subfamily Aurantioideae); older synonyms include Crateva marmelos and Belou marmelos. It is native to the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia, especially India's Eastern Ghats and its central-to-northern states such as Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal, and along the Himalayan foothills, and has naturalised in Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Nepal and Thailand. It is a deciduous shrub or small-to-medium tree to about 13 m, with slender drooping branches, pale brown spiny bark (spines 1.2-2.5 cm), and trifoliate leaves 5-14 cm long that darken from pale to deep green with age; it bears sweetly fragrant pale yellow flowers in drooping clusters. The fruit is globose to pear-shaped with a thick, very hard rind that must be broken open with a hammer or machete, revealing 8-15 aromatic orange pulp segments packed with small hairy seeds in mucilage; it takes about 11 months to ripen. The tree tolerates an unusually wide range of conditions — soil pH from 5 to 10 and temperatures from -7°C to 48°C — and is currently assessed as Near Threatened by the IUCN.

Bael fruit is eaten fresh or made into candy, toffee, pulp powder or nectar, and its strained, sweetened juice — bael sharbat or 'bela pana' — is a popular traditional cooling summer drink in India, rich in vitamin C. In Ayurveda the leaves, bark, roots, fruit and seeds are all used to treat various ailments, and a compound called aegeline, extracted from bael leaves, has been researched for therapeutic uses — though it also drew safety scrutiny after a 2013 outbreak of liver injury (97 reported cases, including some liver transplants and deaths) was linked to the weight-loss supplement OxyElite Pro, which contained aegeline; the exact mechanism of that liver damage was never fully confirmed. Religiously, bael is deeply significant in Hinduism: it is mentioned as early as the Rigveda's Sri Sukta, where it is described as the residence of the goddess Lakshmi, and its trifoliate leaf is seen as symbolising the trident of Lord Shiva, giving the tree the epithet 'Bilvadanda' ('bel-staffed'); its leaves are traditionally offered to Shiva in sets of three. Among the Newar community in Nepal, girls traditionally undergo a symbolic 'marriage' to a bael fruit (Ihi) in a fertility ritual said to protect them from the ill fortune of widowhood so long as the fruit remains uncracked. The tree also appears in Buddhist scripture, in the Daddabha Jataka.
